title: DSA core: interview routine, complexity and hashing
seriesDescription: Complexity and pattern reasoning for hashing, windows, stacks, lists, trees, heaps and graphs, in pseudocode. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Language-independent reasoning for arrays and hashing: the interview routine, complexity analysis, prefix sums and choosing between hashing and sorting.
source: LeetCode problem set and discuss; NeetCode roadmap; Cracking the Coding Interview; CLRS (hash tables, sorting)

questions.prompt: Match each step of the coding-interview routine with what you do in it.

right.text: Ask about input size, duplicates, negatives and what to return when no answer exists
State a simple correct baseline and its cost, so you always have a fallback
Trace the finished code by hand on a small example, tracking every variable
Try empty, single-element, all-equal and maximum-size inputs
Give time and space in terms of n and name the dominant term
Rewrite the solution in a second language

questions.explanation: The order is clarify, brute force, better idea, code, dry run, test, complexity. Interviewers grade the routine as much as the final code; skipping the brute force and the dry run is the most common way to lose points.

questions.text: First {1} the problem and constraints, then state a {2} solution with its cost, look for a better idea, write the code, and {3} it by hand on a small input before declaring it done.
questions.explanation: Constraints drive the target complexity: n up to 10^5 usually means O(n log n) or better, n up to 20 allows exponential search.

questions.prompt: A brute-force two sum checks every pair i < j in an array of 10 elements. How many pair checks happen in the worst case?
questions.explanation: n(n-1)/2 = 10*9/2 = 45. That quadratic growth is why the brute force is too slow for n = 10^5 (about 5 billion pairs) and why you reach for a hash table.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Sorting an array and then finding a pair with a target sum using two pointers is O(n log n) overall.
questions.reason: The two-pointer scan itself is O(n), but sorting costs O(n log n) and dominates.

whys.a: Correct: the total is the sum of the phases, and the largest term wins.
whys.b: Both are true, but R is exactly why the total is O(n log n), so it does explain A.
whys.c: A is true, so this cannot be the answer.
whys.d: A is true, so this cannot be the answer.

questions.explanation: Add the phases and keep the dominant term: O(n log n) + O(n) = O(n log n).

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: After one O(n) pass, a prefix-sum array answers any range-sum query in O(1).
questions.reason: Arrays support O(1) random access by index.

whys.a: R is true but it is not the reason: the O(1) comes from prefix[r+1] - prefix[l].
whys.b: Correct: both are true, but the real reason is the subtraction identity, not random access alone.
whys.c: A is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: sum(l..r) = prefix[r+1] - prefix[l]. The same idea, with a hash table of earlier prefixes, solves "subarray sum equals K".

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Grouping anagrams by the sorted string key costs O(n * k log k) for n words of length k.
questions.reason: Sorting the k characters of one word takes O(k) time.

whys.a: R is false, so this cannot be right.
whys.b: R is false, so no both-true option holds.
whys.c: Correct: A is true (n sorts of cost k log k) but sorting k characters takes O(k log k), not O(k).
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: The alternative key is a 26-count signature, giving O(n * k) for lowercase words. Mention both.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: A hash-table-based two sum is guaranteed O(n) time even in the worst case.
questions.reason: Hash table lookups and inserts take O(1) time on average.

whys.a: A is not true as stated, so no explanation can hold.
whys.b: A is false, so both-true options are out.
whys.c: R is true, so option c cannot hold.
whys.d: Correct: O(1) is an average-case (expected) bound. With many collisions a lookup can degrade (to O(log n) with tree buckets, or O(n) with chains), so the worst case is not O(n).

questions.explanation: Say "expected O(n)" in an interview. It shows you know the difference between expected and worst-case hash costs.

questions.text: Keep a running {1} sum; the number of earlier prefixes equal to {2} is how many subarrays end here; seed the table with prefix {3} seen once so subarrays starting at index 0 count.
questions.explanation: Because values can be negative a sliding window does not work (extending the window does not monotonically grow the sum), so prefix sums with a frequency table are the standard answer.

questions.prompt: How many contiguous subarrays of [3, 4, -3, 1, 2, -1, 2] sum to K = 3?
questions.explanation: They are [3], [4,-3,1,2,-1], [1,2] and [2,-1,2]. The prefix-sum table finds them in O(n); because of the negative numbers a sliding window would not work.

questions.prompt: For nums = [2, 3, 4, 5], the product-except-self array has output[i] equal to the product of all other elements. What is output[1]?
questions.explanation: 2 * 4 * 5 = 40. The O(n) solution without division multiplies a running prefix product on the way right and a running suffix product on the way back, using the output array itself, so extra space is O(1) besides the answer.

questions.prompt: Write pseudocode for two sum: given a list nums and a number target, return the indices of two different elements that add up to target, in one pass using a lookup table from value to index.

checks.label: creates an empty lookup table (map, dictionary or hash table)
loops over the elements with their index
checks the table for the complement before storing the current value

questions.explanation: The order matters: look up the complement first, then store the current element, so an element is never paired with itself. Any readable pseudocode with those four moves is acceptable.

questions.prompt: You must detect whether an array of 10^6 numbers has a duplicate, and the interviewer says extra memory is very tight. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Sort the array in place, then compare neighbours: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space.
options.why: Correct: it trades a log factor of time for almost no extra memory.

options.text: Insert every number into a hash set: O(n) expected time but O(n) extra memory.
options.why: Fast, but it spends exactly the memory the interviewer ruled out.

options.text: Compare every pair of numbers: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space.
options.why: About 5 * 10^11 comparisons is far too slow for n = 10^6.

options.text: Build a balanced search tree and check before each insert: O(n log n) with O(n) extra space.
options.why: It is as slow as sorting and uses more memory than sorting in place.

questions.explanation: State the trade-off aloud: hash set for speed, sort for memory. Ask whether the input may be modified, because in-place sorting changes it.

questions.prompt: Which approaches to "does the array contain a duplicate" run in O(n log n) time or better? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sort, then compare each element with its neighbour.
options.why: Correct: sorting is O(n log n) and the scan is O(n).

options.text: Insert elements into a hash set and test membership before each insert.
Insert elements into a balanced search tree, checking before each insert.
options.why: Correct: n operations at O(log n) each.

questions.explanation: Brute force is the fallback; the other three are the standard improvements with different memory profiles.

questions.prompt: In a coding interview you should skip the brute-force solution and go straight to the optimal one, because stating the brute force wastes time.

options.why: Interviewers expect a baseline first; skipping it hides your reasoning.
Correct: a stated brute force proves you understand the problem, gives a fallback, and often hints at the optimisation.

questions.explanation: Say the brute force and its cost in a sentence or two, then improve it.
